title: Meet D-Rex, a Giant Fungus Whose Family Began 65 Million Years Ago
summary:
Scientists exploring forests in Yunnan, China, have discovered a giant fungus with a dinosaur-sized nickname: D-rex. Its upright reproductive structures can reach 50 cm (20 inches) tall and weigh as much as 2.2 kg (4.9 pounds), making them the largest known fruiting bodies among fungi in the phylum Ascomycota.

The species is called Dianjunus rex, a name inspired by its impressive size and the ancient Dian kingdom. Researchers said it is different enough from known fungi to need a new genus and an entirely new family, Dianjunaceae, within the order Xylariales.

The team found the fungus while surveying temperate coniferous forests near Damaidi and Yipinglang, and tropical rainforest near Nanbang. They spotted unusually large, whitish structures, known as stromata, growing from the woody roots of Chinese cork oak trees.

Ascomycetes make up the largest major group of fungi, with more than 64,000 recognized species. Unlike familiar mushrooms, they do not produce true mushroom structures. Instead, they make spores inside tiny sac-like structures found inside or on their fruiting bodies.

Using a method called a molecular clock, scientists compared the fungus's DNA with genomic information from hundreds of other fungi. Their results suggest the Dianjunaceae family first appeared approximately 65 million years ago, roughly one million years after the mass extinction that eliminated the non-avian dinosaurs.

That timing raises a possibility, said Dr Indunil C Senanayake, of the Kunming Institute of Botany: after the extinction, forests changed dramatically, and large amounts of dead plant material suddenly became available. For wood-associated decomposing fungi, he said, such disruption may have created new ecological opportunities.
why_it_matters: This giant fungus shows how life can seize new chances after a catastrophe, and studying its ancient family helps scientists understand how forests and fungi recovered after the dinosaurs disappeared.

background_read: Fungi are living things that are neither plants nor animals, and many of them feed by breaking down dead wood and other plant material.
Unlike familiar mushrooms, ascomycetes make their spores inside tiny sac-like structures on or inside their fruiting bodies.
Scientists group living things into species, genera and families, and a fungus different enough from all known fungi may need a brand-new genus and family of its own.
By comparing DNA with a molecular clock, researchers can estimate when a family first appeared, even from a very long time ago.
